es.summary: Pérdida de sangre del intestino delgado o grueso que puede ser aguda o crónica y se manifiesta con cambios en las heces y signos de hipovolemia.
key_points: Puede presentarse con heces melena o hematochezia según la localización.
La pérdida sanguínea provoca déficit de volumen y desequilibrio electrolítico.
Laboratorio: Hb <10 g/dL, hematocrito bajo, BUN/creatinina elevado.
El manejo incluye reposición de líquidos, transfusión y control endoscópico del foco.

pathophysiology: Lesión de la mucosa intestinal produce ruptura de vasos sanguíneos.
La sangre se mezcla con el contenido intestinal y se elimina por heces o vómito.
La pérdida de sangre reduce el volumen intravascular, activando la respuesta compensatoria catecolaminérgica.
risk_factors: Varices esofágicas o gástricas por hipertensión portal.
Enfermedad inflamatoria intestinal (enfermedad de Crohn, colitis ulcerosa).
Uso de AINES, anticoagulantes o antiagregantes.
signs_symptoms: Vómito con sangre o aspecto de café molido.
Hipotensión ortostática, taquicardia, piel fría y húmeda.
Disminución de la diuresis y mareos.
diagnostics: BUN y creatinina: aumento del BUN/creatinina indica hipovolemia.
Pruebas de sangre oculta en heces si el sangrado es oculto.
Endoscopia digestiva alta o colonoscopia para localizar el foco.
treatment: Reposición de volumen con cristaloides (solución salina al 0.9%).
Transfusión de concentrado de glóbulos rojos si Hb <7 g/dL o síntomas.
Inhibidores de bomba de protones: omeprazol, pantoprazol.
Antifibrinolítico: tranexámico en sangrado por úlcera.
complications: Insuficiencia renal aguda por perfusión disminuida.
nursing_care: Monitorizar signos vitales cada 15‑30 min y presión arterial invasiva si está indicada.
Evaluar ingesta y salida; registrar diuresis cada hora.
Observar color y consistencia de heces y vómitos.
Mantener acceso venoso de gran calibre y administrar fluidos según prescripción.
Preparar al paciente para endoscopia: ayuno y consentimiento.
patient_teaching: Explicar la importancia de reportar cualquier cambio en el color de heces o vómitos.
Instruir sobre la adherencia a la medicación antiácida y evitar AINES sin indicación.
Enseñar signos de alarma: mareos, palidez, disminución de la orina.
Promover una dieta blanda y evitar irritantes gástricos durante la recuperación.

outcomes: Balance hídrico: ingesta y salida equilibradas en 24 h

interventions.action: Evaluar signos vitales y nivel de conciencia cada 15 minutos
interventions.rationale: Detectar rápidamente deterioro hemodinámico

interventions.action: Registrar ingesta y salida, incluyendo diuresis y pérdidas gastrointestinales
interventions.rationale: Permite calcular el balance hídrico y ajustar la terapia

interventions.action: Administrar cristaloides IV según prescripción y monitorizar respuesta
interventions.rationale: Restituye el volumen intravascular y mejora perfusión

interventions.action: Preparar y administrar transfusión de concentrado de glóbulos rojos si está indicada
interventions.rationale: Corrige la anemia y aumenta la capacidad de transporte de oxígeno

interventions.action: Colaborar con el médico para iniciar inhibidores de bomba de protones IV
interventions.rationale: Reduce la acidez y favorece la hemostasia de úlceras

interventions.action: Educar al paciente sobre la importancia de reportar cualquier sangrado nuevo
interventions.rationale: Facilita la detección precoz de re‑sangrado

related_to: reposiciones masivas de cristaloides sin electrolitos

interventions.action: Obtener y registrar electrolitos séricos cada 6‑8 horas
interventions.rationale: Detectar alteraciones tempranas y guiar la reposición

interventions.action: Administrar soluciones con electrolitos (por ejemplo, Ringer lactato) según prescripción
interventions.rationale: Previene hiponatremia e hipocalemia durante la reposición de volumen

interventions.action: Evaluar estado neurológico (confusión, debilidad muscular) cada turno
interventions.rationale: Los desequilibrios electrolíticos pueden manifestarse con alteraciones neurológicas

interventions.action: Colaborar para reemplazar potasio o magnesio si los valores están bajos
interventions.rationale: Mantener la función cardíaca y muscular

interventions.action: Enseñar al paciente la importancia de una dieta rica en potasio (plátano, papaya) cuando sea apropiado
interventions.rationale: Apoya la reposición natural de electrolitos

en.summary: Loss of blood from the small or large intestine that can be acute or chronic and presents with changes in stool and signs of hypovolemia.
key_points: May present with melena or hematochezia depending on location.
Blood loss causes volume deficit and electrolyte imbalance.
Lab: Hb <10 g/dL, low hematocrit, elevated BUN/creatinine.
Management includes fluid replacement, transfusion, and endoscopic control of the source.

pathophysiology: Intestinal mucosal injury causes rupture of blood vessels.
Blood mixes with intestinal contents and is eliminated via stool or vomit.
Blood loss reduces intravascular volume, triggering catecholamine compensatory response.
risk_factors: Esophageal or gastric varices from portal hypertension.
Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis).
Use of NSAIDs, anticoagulants, or antiplatelets.
signs_symptoms: Vomiting with blood or coffee‑ground appearance.
Orthostatic hypotension, tachycardia, cold and clammy skin.
diagnostics: BUN and creatinine: increased BUN/creatinine indicates hypovolemia.
Fecal occult blood test if bleeding is occult.
Upper GI endoscopy or colonoscopy to locate the source.
treatment: Volume replacement with crystalloids (0.9% saline solution).
Red blood cell concentrate transfusion if Hb <7 g/dL or symptomatic.
Antifibrinolytic: tranexamic acid for ulcer bleeding.
complications: Acute renal failure from decreased perfusion.
nursing_care: Monitor vital signs every 15‑30 minutes and invasive blood pressure if indicated.
Assess intake and output; record urine hourly.
Observe stool and vomit color and consistency.
Maintain large‑bore IV access and administer fluids per order.
Prepare patient for endoscopy: fasting and consent.
patient_teaching: Explain importance of reporting any change in stool or vomit color.
Instruct on adherence to antacid medication and avoid NSAIDs without indication.
Teach warning signs: dizziness, pallor, decreased urine output.
Encourage a bland diet and avoid gastric irritants during recovery.

outcomes: Fluid balance: intake and output equal in 24 h

interventions.action: Assess vital signs and level of consciousness every 15 minutes
interventions.rationale: Detect rapid hemodynamic deterioration

interventions.action: Record intake and output, including urine and GI losses
interventions.rationale: Allows calculation of fluid balance and therapy adjustment

interventions.action: Administer IV crystalloids per order and monitor response
interventions.rationale: Restores intravascular volume and improves perfusion

interventions.action: Prepare and administer packed red blood cell transfusion if indicated
interventions.rationale: Corrects anemia and increases oxygen transport capacity

interventions.action: Collaborate with physician to initiate IV proton pump inhibitors
interventions.rationale: Reduces acidity and promotes ulcer hemostasis

interventions.action: Educate patient on importance of reporting any new bleeding
interventions.rationale: Facilitates early detection of re‑bleeding

interventions.action: Obtain and record serum electrolytes every 6‑8 hours
interventions.rationale: Detect early changes and guide replacement

interventions.action: Administer electrolyte solutions (e.g., Ringer lactate) per order
interventions.rationale: Prevents hyponatremia and hypokalemia during volume replacement

interventions.action: Assess neurological status (confusion, muscle weakness) each shift
interventions.rationale: Electrolyte imbalances may manifest with neurological changes

interventions.action: Collaborate to replace potassium or magnesium if values are low
interventions.rationale: Maintain cardiac and muscular function

interventions.action: Teach patient the importance of a potassium‑rich diet (banana, papaya) when appropriate
interventions.rationale: Supports natural electrolyte replenishment

sources.name: Maternal-Newborn Nursing: Conditions Limited to Pregnancy

key_points.3.quote: Patients with GI bleeding may require IV fluid replacement or multiple blood transfusions to restore lost blood volume (DiGregorio & Alvey, 2022).

sections.risk_factors.0.quote: One of the main causes of GI bleeding is the presence of bleeding stress ulcers, usually in the stomach or intestines.

sections.risk_factors.1.quote: Another common cause of GI bleeding is related to esophageal varices : small veins that form when portal hypertension is present, often due to alcoholic cirrhosis liver disease.

sections.signs_symptoms.0.quote: Common assessment findings for patients with acute GI bleeding are: abdominal pain or cramping anemia cool, clammy skin decreased LOC decreased urine output hematemesis (bloody vomitus) hypoactive bowel sounds hypotension melena (bloody stools) and/or dark tarry stools tachycardia Medical A

sections.signs_symptoms.2.quote: Common assessment findings for patients with acute GI bleeding are: abdominal pain or cramping anemia cool, clammy skin decreased LOC decreased urine output hematemesis (bloody vomitus) hypoactive bowel sounds hypotension melena (bloody stools) and/or dark tarry stools tachycardia Medical A

sections.treatment.2.quote: Most patients experiencing bleeding from stress ulcers will also be recommended to take a PPI such as omeprazole (e.g., Prilosec) or pantoprazole (Protonix) to decrease gastric acid secretion and allow for complete healing of the ulcer.

sections.treatment.3.quote: If the bleeding originates from esophageal varices, octreotide (Sandostatin) can be used to stop the bleeding.
